fun_facts: UK's most widespread bumblebee. Queens can be seen flying on mild days even in winter. Colonies can number several hundred workers.
Nearly identical to the buff-tailed bumblebee but with a pure white tail instead of buff. Actually a group of very similar species that need close examination to tell apart.
Females are jet black with a bright orange-red tail. Often nests under stones or in old walls — the species name 'lapidarius' means 'of stones'.
Ginger and fluffy, with one of the longest flight seasons of any UK bumblebee, from February right through to November.
Has the longest tongue of any UK bumblebee, letting it reach deep into tubular flowers like foxgloves that other bees can't access.
One of the first bumblebees on the wing each year, often emerging in February. Small colonies of only 50-100 workers, much smaller than other bumblebee species.
First recorded in the UK in 2001 and has since spread across most of the country. Unusually for a bumblebee, it often nests above ground in bird boxes and roof spaces.
Females are strikingly foxy-orange and dig neat volcano-shaped mounds of soil in lawns each spring — often mistaken for ant hills.
One of the earliest bees to emerge each spring and a superb pollinator of fruit trees. Nests readily in hollow stems and bee hotels.
Fast, hovering flight makes it look like a tiny hummingbird. Males and females look completely different — males are sandy-coloured, females are all black.
Striking grey-and-black banded bee, sometimes nesting in large aggregations of hundreds of burrows in short grass or bare soil.
Cuts neat semi-circular discs from rose and other leaves to line its nest cells — the tell-tale scalloped leaf edges are a classic sign of its presence.
Females scrape soft plant hairs, especially from lamb's ear (Stachys), to felt into nest material. Males aggressively guard patches of flowers from rival bees.
Tiny, metallic-sheened ground-nester found almost everywhere in the UK. Some furrow bee species show early social behaviour, a step between solitary and colonial living.
Produces two generations a year, one in spring and one in summer — unusual among mining bees, which typically fly for just a few weeks.
Nests inside empty snail shells, which the female then camouflages by covering with a thatch of grass and plant stems, sometimes carried some distance.
One of Britain's largest mining bees. Nationally scarce and tightly linked to scabious flowers, from which females collect almost all of their pollen.
A declining chalk-grassland specialist, now largely confined to a handful of sites in southern England after major losses through the 20th century.
Once widespread across the UK, now mostly restricted to coastal grassland, machair, and moorland after a significant 20th-century decline.
HOST PLANT: ivy (Hedera helix). One of the latest bees on the wing each year, timing its whole flight period, September to November, to match ivy's autumn bloom. First recorded in Britain in 2001.
HOST PLANT: willow (Salix spp., including goat willow). One of the very first bees to emerge each year, often flying in late winter to catch the first willow catkins.
HOST PLANT: devil's-bit scabious and field scabious. A UK conservation-priority species, now restricted to a small number of scabious-rich sites.
HOST PLANT: yellow loosestrife. Uniquely among UK bees, collects floral oils as well as pollen from its host plant, using the oil to waterproof its underground nest cells.
HOST PLANT: harebell and other Campanula species. Tiny, barely bigger than an ant, and almost never seen away from its host flowers.
Tiny bee, only 5-5.5mm long, that builds its nest partitions entirely from pine resin. Forages mainly on yellow daisy-family flowers like ragwort and fleabane.
HOST PLANT: harebell and other Campanula species. Flies for a short window, mid-July to late August, exactly matching Campanula bloom time. Restricted mainly to chalk grassland and woodland rides.
One of the most widespread and abundant spring mining bees in the UK, found in gardens, hedgerows, and woodland edges nearly everywhere. Forages on a wide range of spring blossom.
